title: Is yogurt a miracle food?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore yogurt: its accidental origins in the Middle East and Turkey (the word comes from Turkish yogurmak, "to thicken"), its spread to Europe and the US through Dannon (which moved to the Bronx and introduced fruit-on-the-bottom), the FDA and National Yogurt Association live-culture standards, how yogurt is made (pasteurizing, homogenizing, adding bacteria at around 115 F), how the bacteria help lactose intolerant people digest lactose and aid protein and folate, the health claims and weak evidence behind them (including a Wisconsin inflammation study funded by the National Dairy Council), weight loss caveats, sugar in kids' yogurts, and the Dannon "In Soviet Georgia" ad campaign. The episode closes with a listener mail about Robin Hood and King Richard and King John history.

segments.title: Opening banter about yogurt
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether they like yogurt and fruit on the bottom, their yogurt habits, and honey with Greek yogurt. They preview the episode and mention a past probiotics episode.

segments.title: History of yogurt origins and spread
segments.summary: Yogurt likely began accidentally in the Middle East thousands of years ago when milk was stored in animal containers and soured. Its tangy form was tolerated by lactose intolerant people and helped civilization grow. The word yogurt is Turkish, and Turkey likely spread yogurt to Europe and India. Turkish per-capita consumption is compared with US consumption.

segments.title: Yogurt arrives in America with Dannon
segments.summary: Yogurt spread to Europe in the late nineteenth century and reached the US in the twentieth century. Dannon moved operations from Spain to the Bronx and popularized yogurt in America, with fruit on the bottom helping it take off, and later Greek-style yogurt became popular.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the probiotics discussion.

segments.title: Probiotics and live cultures standards
segments.summary: Probiotics are beneficial bacteria that replenish gut flora. Yogurt must meet National Yogurt Association and FDA standards, including a minimum of 100 million bacteria per gram and specific strains: Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus. Some bacteria survive stomach acid by pumping acid out.

segments.title: Tangent on neti pots and water boiling
segments.summary: Josh describes his neti pot routine and the hosts discuss how long water should be boiled to kill pathogens, including altitude adjustments. The conversation ends with a joke about the brain-eating amoeba risk.

segments.title: How yogurt is made
segments.summary: Milk is separated into cream and skim, thickened with milk powder or gelatin, pasteurized briefly at about 171 F, and homogenized. It is cooled to about 115 F and then bacteria are added to ferment the milk into yogurt. The hosts note an upcoming homogenization/pasteurization discussion.

segments.title: Lactose intolerance and nutrients in yogurt
segments.summary: Bacteria in yogurt metabolize lactose into lactic acid and release an enzyme that helps people digest lactose, so many lactose intolerant people can eat yogurt. The bacteria also make protein more bioavailable and produce folate.

segments.title: Fruit on the bottom and the FDA
segments.summary: Dannon's fruit-on-the-bottom idea was reportedly suggested by Wan Metzker, son of a Dannon co-founder, and the USDA initially objected to mixing fruit with dairy. Placing fruit on the bottom was allowed as not mixing.

segments.title: Yogurt health claims and evidence
segments.summary: Yogurt is linked in studies to many benefits, but evidence is mixed and inconclusive. Calcium, vitamin D, protein, potassium, and riboflavin are real benefits. Low-fat yogurt may aid weight loss through fullness, but low-fat versions often add sugar, artificial sweeteners, or sodium. A University of Wisconsin-Madison study of sixty women, funded by the National Dairy Council, found some inflammation marker improvements, but not a cure for rheumatoid arthritis. Kids' yogurts are often high in sugar.

segments.title: Traditional yogurt varieties and Dannon's In Soviet Georgia ad
segments.summary: Greek yogurt is the closest US option to traditional yogurt, and Bulgarian yogurt is also noted. Dannon's 1997 In Soviet Georgia ad campaign featured elderly people in the Soviet republic of Georgia and is credited with boosting yogurt sales in America.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up by encouraging listeners to eat yogurt and invite listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail on Robin Hood history
segments.summary: Listener Stephen Gray corrects and expands the Robin Hood episode: Richard was king for ten years but spent only six months in England, John schemed against him, and the Robin Hood stories may reflect Henry III's heavy taxation for the war in Gascony.
